questions.q: (a) What are the phases of the Moon? (b) Name the phase in which less than half of the Moon's illuminated portion is seen from the Earth.
questions.a: (a) The phases of the Moon are the changing shapes of the bright portion of the Moon from one day to another, as seen from the Earth. (b) The crescent phase.
s: (a) States that phases are the day-to-day changing shapes of the Moon's bright portion as seen from the Earth
(b) Names the crescent phase

questions.q: True or False? Give the reason. 'When we see a thin crescent Moon, less than half of the Moon's surface is being lit by the Sun.'
questions.a: False. The half of the Moon that faces the Sun is always lit. We see a crescent because only a small part of that lit half faces the Earth, so less than half of the illuminated portion is seen.
s: States the verdict: False
Explains that half the Moon is always lit and a crescent shows only a small part of the lit half that faces the Earth

questions.q: In a model of the Moon's phases, a ball on a stick stands for the Moon, a lamp for the Sun and a student's head for the Earth. The student holds the ball at arm's length and turns slowly. (a) When the ball is held towards the lamp, can she see its lit part? Which Moon day does this match? (b) When the ball is held opposite to the lamp, how much of the lit part does she see? Which Moon day does this match? (c) At the in-between positions, what does the line separating the lit and unlit parts look like?
questions.a: (a) No; she faces only the unlit part of the ball, as on the new Moon day (Amavasya). (b) She sees the entire lit portion, as on the full Moon day (Purnima). (c) The line looks curved.
s: (a) Says the lit part cannot be seen and matches it to the new Moon day
(b) Says the entire lit portion is seen and matches it to the full Moon day
(c) States that the dividing line appears curved

questions.q:
A planetarium in Mysuru shows the Moon moving around the Earth through eight equally spaced positions, A to H, in order. Position A is directly opposite the Sun and position E is directly towards the Sun. The show labels the positions with day numbers: A Day 1, B Day 4, C Day 8, D Day 12, E Day 15, F Day 18, G Day 22, H Day 26, and the Moon is back at A after about a month.
(a) On which day number is the Moon a new Moon?
(b) Name the phase seen from the Earth on Day 4 and on Day 18.
(c) From Day 15 to Day 22, is the bright part growing or shrinking, and what is this period called in India?
(d) A visitor wants to see exactly half of the illuminated portion while the bright part is growing. Which day number should she choose? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Day 15 (position E): the Moon is towards the Sun, so only its non-illuminated half faces the Earth. (b) Day 4 (B): gibbous, more than half of the illuminated portion is seen; Day 18 (F): crescent, less than half is seen. (c) Growing; this is the waxing period, called Shukla Paksha. (d) Day 22 (position G). Half of the illuminated portion is seen at C (Day 8) and at G (Day 22), but the bright part shrinks from A to E and grows from E back to A, so only Day 22 fits.
s: (a) Identifies Day 15 (E, towards the Sun) as the new Moon
(b) Names gibbous for Day 4 and crescent for Day 18
(c) Says growing and names it waxing / Shukla Paksha
(d) Chooses Day 22, ruling out Day 8 because the bright part is shrinking then

Consider the statements.
I. The Moon always rises and sets at different times from the Sun.
II. A waxing Moon is easiest to spot at sunrise.
III. On the new Moon day, the Moon appears closest to the Sun in the sky.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only

questions.q: True or False? Give the reason. 'The phases of the Moon happen because the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.'
questions.a: False. The phases happen because the relative positions of the Sun, Moon and Earth change as the Moon revolves around the Earth, so we see a changing part of its lit half. The Earth's shadow on the Moon causes a lunar eclipse, not the phases.
s: States the verdict: False
Gives the real cause (changing relative positions as the Moon revolves) and says the Earth's shadow causes a lunar eclipse

questions.q: A Chennai newspaper lists moonrise at 13:40 on Friday and at 14:31 on Saturday. (a) Using the delay between these two days, predict Sunday's moonrise time. (b) Kiran wants to see the Moon in the eastern sky on Sunday afternoon. From about what time can she expect to see it? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) The delay is 14:31 - 13:40 = 51 minutes, so Sunday's moonrise is about 14:31 + 51 minutes = 15:22. (b) From about 15:52. Just after the listed moonrise the Moon is too low; she may need to wait about 30 minutes for it to climb high enough to be seen.
s: (a) Finds the 51-minute delay and predicts about 15:22
(b) Adds about 30 minutes for the Moon to climb high enough: about 15:52

questions.q: (a) At what time of day is a waxing Moon easiest to spot? (b) At what time of day is a waning Moon easiest to spot? (c) On a full Moon day, where is the Moon when the Sun rises in the East?
questions.a: (a) At sunset. (b) At sunrise. (c) The Moon is almost setting in the West, nearly opposite the Sun.
s: (a) Sunset for the waxing Moon
(b) Sunrise for the waning Moon
(c) Almost setting in the West, nearly opposite the Sun

questions.q:
A school astronomy club in Indore notes the time at which the Moon is highest in the sky on four nights in a row: Monday 20:20, Tuesday 21:12, Wednesday 22:01, Thursday 22:50 (figures illustrative). The school gate closes at 23:00, and the club wants to show a visiting guest the Moon at its highest before the gate closes.
(a) Find the average daily delay in the time the Moon is highest.
(b) Why does the Moon reach the same spot in the sky later each day, although the Earth rotates once in 24 hours?
(c) Using your answer to (a), predict the time on Friday.
(d) The guest can come only on Thursday or on Friday. Which day should the club choose? Justify with times.
questions.a: (a) The delays are 52, 49 and 49 minutes; average = 150 / 3 = 50 minutes. (b) While the Earth rotates once, the Moon moves ahead a little in its orbit around the Earth, so the Earth has to rotate some more before the Moon is back in nearly the same spot. (c) 22:50 + 50 minutes = 23:40 on Friday. (d) Thursday: the Moon is highest at 22:50, just before the gate closes at 23:00. On Friday it is highest at about 23:40, 40 minutes after the gate closes.
s: (a) Finds the delays 52, 49, 49 and the average 50 minutes
(b) Explains that the Moon moves ahead in its orbit during one rotation, so the Earth must turn a little more
(c) Predicts about 23:40 on Friday
(d) Chooses Thursday (22:50, before 23:00), showing Friday (about 23:40) is too late

questions.q: Answer each part in one or two lines. (a) Today the Moon rises at 17:35. At about what time will it rise tomorrow? (b) Whose shadow falls on the Moon during a lunar eclipse? (c) On which kind of Moon day can a solar eclipse happen? (d) Why do eclipses not happen every month? (e) On which day does the Moon appear farthest from the Sun in the sky?

(d) Because the Moon's orbit is slightly tilted with respect to the Earth's orbit around the Sun, so the three bodies do not line up on most full and new Moon days. (e) The full Moon day.
s: (a) Adds about 50 minutes to get about 18:25
(b) Names the Earth's shadow
(c) Names the new Moon day
(d) Gives the slight tilt of the Moon's orbit
(e) Names the full Moon day

questions.q:
Between two harvests that fall at the same point in the seasons, the elders of a village count 365 sunrises. Consider the statements.
I. The sunrises they count come round once for every rotation of the Earth about its own axis.
II. During those 365 days, the Moon goes through its full cycle of phases about 12 times.
III. Since the Earth goes round the Sun in exactly 365 days, their harvest day will stay at the same point in the seasons for ever.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only

questions.q: True or False? Give the reason. 'The full Moon falls on 10 May this year, so the next full Moon will fall on about 8 June.'
questions.a: True. The Moon takes about 29.5 days to cycle through all its phases. 10 May + 29 days = 8 June (and + 30 days = 9 June), so the next full Moon falls on about 8 or 9 June.
s: States the verdict: True
Uses the 29.5-day phase cycle: 10 May + 29 or 30 days = 8 or 9 June

questions.q: Using a correct clock, a student records the time of the shortest shadow of an upright stick on two sunny days in a row: 12:20 on Monday and 13:05 on Tuesday. Show that this record must contain a mistake.
questions.a: The time from one shortest shadow to the next is the length of a solar day. Here it is 24 hours 45 minutes. But the Sun takes about 24 hours (the mean solar day) to return to its highest position, so on Tuesday the shortest shadow should come within a minute or so of 12:20, not at 13:05. So one of the readings is wrong.
s: States that the gap between shortest shadows on two days is one solar day
Finds the recorded gap of 24 hours 45 minutes
Compares it with the mean solar day of about 24 hours and concludes a reading is wrong

questions.q:
Ishaan in Jaipur tests his new wristwatch against the Sun. Each day he notes the time of the shortest shadow of an upright stick on his watch, while his sister notes it on the school's radio clock, which is known to be correct. Monday: watch 12:20, clock 12:20. Tuesday: watch 12:25, clock 12:20. Wednesday: watch 12:30, clock 12:20 (figures illustrative).
(a) How long is one solar day by the radio clock, and how long does it appear to be by the watch?
(b) Which device keeps time with the Sun, and by how much does the other one gain each day?
(c) If Ishaan does not correct the watch, by how many minutes will it be wrong one week after Monday?
(d) How can he use the stick alone to correct the watch each day?
questions.a: (a) Radio clock: 24 hours (12:20 to 12:20). Watch: 24 hours 5 minutes. (b) The radio clock keeps time with the Sun; the watch gains 5 minutes every day. (c) 7 x 5 = 35 minutes fast. (d) The Sun returns to its highest position about every 24 hours, so each day he can reset the watch to 12:20 at the moment the stick's shadow is shortest.
s: (a) 24 hours by the radio clock and 24 hours 5 minutes by the watch
(b) Radio clock keeps time; watch gains 5 minutes a day
(c) 7 x 5 = 35 minutes fast
(d) Resets the watch to 12:20 when the shadow is shortest

questions.q: Answer each part in one line. (a) An upright stick's shadow was shortest at 12:22 on Monday and at 12:21 on Tuesday (figures illustrative). How long was that solar day? (b) The mean solar day is the average time between which two events? (c) Which unit of time is based on the cycle of the Moon's phases? (d) Which natural cycle does the Earth go through once in each revolution around the Sun, and which unit of time does it define? (e) About how many days does the Moon take to go through all its phases twice?
questions.a: (a) 23 hours 59 minutes (one minute less than 24 hours). (b) The Sun being at its highest position in the sky on one day and at its highest position on the next day. (c) The month. (d) One cycle of seasons; it defines the solar year. (e) 2 x 29.5 = 59 days.
s: (a) 23 hours 59 minutes
(b) Sun's highest position on one day to its highest position the next day
(c) The month
(d) One cycle of seasons, defining the solar year
(e) About 59 days

questions.q: (a) What is Adhika Maasa? (b) Why is it added in a luni-solar calendar?
questions.a: (a) Adhika Maasa is an extra (intercalary) month added to the year every few years. (b) Twelve lunar months make 354 days, nearly 11 days short of the solar year; every 2-3 years this gap grows to nearly a month, so the extra month keeps the calendar in step with the seasons.
s: (a) Defines Adhika Maasa as an extra (intercalary) month added every few years
(b) Explains it makes up the gap of about 11 days a year between 12 lunar months and the solar year

questions.q: True or False? Give the reason. 'The year 2200 will be a leap year in the Gregorian calendar, because 2200 is divisible by four.'
questions.a: False. Leap years are skipped every 100 years (as in 1700, 1800 and 1900) and added back only every 400 years (as in 1600 and 2000). 2200 is a century year that is not divisible by 400, so it will not be a leap year.
s: States the verdict: False
Applies the 100-year skip and 400-year add-back rule to 2200

questions.q: True or False? Give the reason. 'Astronomers use the sidereal year to keep track of the Earth's position in its orbit around the Sun.'
questions.a: True. The sidereal year is the time for the same stars to rise again at sunset, and in modern times astronomers use it to keep track of the Earth's position in its orbit.
s: States the verdict: True
Describes the sidereal year (same stars rising again at sunset) and its use by astronomers

questions.q: Ritu says: 'A luni-solar calendar counts its days and months by the phases of the Moon, so, like a purely lunar calendar, its months drift away from the seasons.' Is Ritu right, wrong or partly right? Explain which part of her statement is correct and which is not.
questions.a: Partly right. The first part is correct: a luni-solar calendar mainly uses the Moon's phases to count its days and months. The second part is wrong: unlike a purely lunar calendar, it adds an extra month (Adhika Maasa) every few years, when the gap of about 11 days a year has grown close to a month. This keeps it in step with the seasons, so festivals that follow it shift by typically less than a month on the Gregorian calendar.
s: Gives the verdict: partly right
Accepts the first part: months and days are counted by the Moon's phases
Rejects the second part: Adhika Maasa is added every few years, so it stays in step with the seasons and does not drift like a lunar calendar

questions.q: About the Indian National Calendar: (a) On which Gregorian date does its year begin in a regular year? (b) On which Gregorian date does it begin in a leap year? (c) To which of its months is the extra day added in a leap year?
questions.a: (a) 22 March. (b) 21 March. (c) Chaitra, the first month.
s: (a) 22 March
(b) 21 March
(c) Chaitra

questions.q:
A railway museum in Kolkata has an old ticket register that runs from 1 January 1896 to 31 December 1912, with one page for each day. The curator wants to check that no page is missing. She first lists the years in the span that are divisible by four, and then applies the Gregorian leap-year rules.
(a) List the years from 1896 to 1912 that are divisible by four.
(b) Which of these years was not a leap year in the Gregorian calendar, and why?
(c) How many leap days fall in the span?
(d) How many pages should the register have in all?
questions.a: (a) 1896, 1900, 1904, 1908 and 1912. (b) 1900: leap years are skipped every 100 years (like 1700, 1800, 1900) unless the year is one of the 400-year years (like 1600, 2000). (c) 4 leap days (1896, 1904, 1908, 1912). (d) The span has 17 years, so 17 x 365 + 4 = 6205 + 4 = 6209 pages.
s: (b) Names 1900 and gives the 100-year skip rule
(c) Counts 4 leap days
(d) Computes 17 x 365 + 4 = 6209 pages

questions.q:
A new boarding school in the Nilgiris is choosing one calendar for its year planner. It needs (i) a sports week that falls in the same season every year, and (ii) a sky-watch night on every full Moon.
(a) How long is a year of 12 lunar months, and what does a lunar calendar use to fix its months?
(b) Show with numbers how far the sports week of a purely lunar calendar drifts against the seasons in two years.
(c) Why does a solar calendar such as the Gregorian calendar meet need (i), but not by itself tell when full Moons fall?
(d) How does a luni-solar calendar try to meet both needs?
(e) The planner team is split between the Gregorian calendar with a printed list of full Moon dates, and a luni-solar calendar. Which would you choose? Justify, naming one weakness of each.
questions.a: (a) About 354 days; its months follow the phases of the Moon (about 29.5 days each). (b) The seasons repeat in about 365 days, so the lunar year falls about 365 - 354 = 11 days short each year; in two years that is 2 x 11 = 22 days, so the sports week has already moved about three weeks against the seasons and keeps drifting. (c) Its months add up to 365 days with a leap day every four years, so it stays in step with the seasons; but its months are not tied to the Moon, so full Moons fall on different dates each year. (d) It counts months by the Moon's phases but adds an extra month (Adhika Maasa) every few years, when the gap nears a month, to keep in step with the seasons. (e) Either choice with a fair reason: the Gregorian calendar keeps the sports week on fixed dates, but the full Moon list must be looked up every year; the luni-solar calendar keeps full Moons on fixed days of its months, but the sports week shifts on the Gregorian dates (by up to about a month) from year to year.
s: (a) About 354 days, with months following the Moon's phases
(b) Shows the 11-day yearly gap adds to 22 days in two years, so the week drifts
(c) Solar months plus leap day follow the seasons; months not tied to the Moon's phases
(d) Moon-based months with Adhika Maasa added every few years
(e) Makes a choice and justifies it with one weakness of each calendar

questions.q: A festival fell on 12 April one year and on 1 April the next year (dates illustrative). (a) Does it follow a solar sidereal calendar or a calendar tied to the phases of the Moon? (b) The 11 days (12 April - 1 April) is the gap between the seasons' year of about 365 days and the lunar year of 12 lunar months, 354 days.

questions.q: True or False? Give the reason. 'A festival that follows a luni-solar calendar can move by two or three months on the Gregorian calendar from one year to the next.'
questions.a: False. For festivals based on luni-solar calendars, the shift is typically less than a month, because these calendars add an intercalary month every few years to correct for the difference between the lunar and the solar year.
s: States the verdict: False

questions.q: (a) Name two festivals that follow a solar sidereal calendar. (b) Name two festivals that are tied to the phases of the Moon. (c) Which of these two groups falls on almost the same Gregorian date every year?

(b) Names two Moon-phase festivals
(c) Picks the solar sidereal group

questions.q:
A kite workshop in Ahmedabad makes kites for the kite festival on Makar Sankranti, which fell on 14 January this year. A sweet shop in Varanasi makes sweets for Diwali, which this year fell on the new Moon of Kartika. Both want their stock ready 10 days before their festival every year for the next five years, and both must order raw material a month before that.
(a) Which kind of calendar does Makar Sankranti follow?
(b) Why can the sweet shop not use one fixed Gregorian date for Diwali every year?
(c) About how far can Diwali's Gregorian date shift from one year to another, and why is the shift limited?
(d) Which business can fix its order dates for all five years today, and what should the other do each year? Justify.
questions.a: (a) A solar sidereal calendar. (b) Diwali is fixed by a phase of the Moon (the new Moon of Kartika) in a luni-solar calendar, and the same phase falls on different Gregorian dates each year. (c) Typically less than a month, because the luni-solar calendar adds an intercalary month every few years to correct for the gap between the lunar and solar years. (d) The kite workshop: Makar Sankranti falls on almost the same Gregorian date every year (it moves only about one day in 71 years), so it can fix all five order dates now. The sweet shop should find each year's Diwali date in advance, for example from the Rashtriya Panchang, which gives festival dates ahead of time, and order a month before that.
s: (a) Names the solar sidereal calendar
(b) Links Diwali to a Moon phase in a luni-solar calendar, so its Gregorian date changes
(c) Typically less than a month, limited by the intercalary month
(d) Chooses the kite workshop and says the sweet shop must check each year's date in advance

questions.q: Kiran in Bhubaneswar notes where the Sun rises at different times of the year. Answer each part in one line. (i) On 10 September, is the Sun in its Uttarayan or its Dakshinayan period? (ii) On 10 May, does the Sun rise a little north of East or a little south of East? (iii) On 5 January, does the Sun rise a little north of East or a little south of East? s: (i) Dakshinayan (June to December)
(ii) North of East
(iii) South of East
(iv) Around 21 June (solstice)

questions.q:
Festivals such as Makar Sankranti, Pongal and Puthandu follow a solar sidereal calendar, while the Gregorian calendar follows the tropical year. The chapter says that Makar Sankranti moves ahead by one day every 71 years.
(a) Between which two kinds of year is the small difference that causes this drift, which is longer, and by about how much?
(b) About how many years would Makar Sankranti take to move ahead by a whole month of 30 days?
(c) Why does Pongal still fall on almost the same Gregorian date from one year to the next?
(d) Eid-ul-Fitr follows the phases of the Moon. Over the same span of years, would it stay in the same Gregorian month? Give the reason.
(e) Puthandu fell on 14 April this year (take this as given). At the chapter's rate of drift, will it still fall in April 300 years from now? Show your working.
questions.a: (a) The sidereal year and the tropical year; the sidereal year is longer, by about 20 minutes. (b) 30 x 71 = 2130 years. (c) The drift is only one day in 71 years, so from one year to the next the shift is a tiny fraction of a day and the date stays almost the same. (d) No. A Moon-based (purely lunar) festival is not corrected to the seasons, so it moves to a different Gregorian date every year and can occur in different months year after year. (e) 300 / 71 is about 4.2, so it moves ahead about 4 days, to about 18 April: still in April.
s: (a) Sidereal and tropical years; sidereal longer by about 20 minutes
(c) One day in 71 years is too small to change the date from year to year
(d) No; a Moon-based festival moves to different months year after year
(e) Finds about 4 days of drift, about 18 April, still in April

questions.q:
Floods have hit 40 villages along a river in Assam (figures illustrative). The state disaster cell must quickly find which fields, roads and homes are under water. Plan X: send 8 survey teams by road; each team can check 2 villages a day, but half the roads are cut. Plan Y: use the latest satellite images of the whole district from India's national mapping platform, which can be ready by the next day.
(a) Which use of artificial satellites named in the chapter does this case show?
(b) Name this mapping platform and the ISRO satellite series whose images it uses, and give two things it shows.
(c) If every road were open, how many days would Plan X take for all 40 villages? Why will it take longer here?
(d) Which plan should the cell use first? Justify, and say what the survey teams are still needed for.
questions.a: (a) Disaster management. (b) Bhuvan, which uses images from ISRO's Cartosat series; any two of terrain, soil, land use and vegetation. (c) 8 teams x 2 villages = 16 villages a day; 40 / 16 = 2.5, so 3 days. With half the roads cut, teams cannot reach many villages, so it will take longer. (d) Plan Y first: it covers the whole district by the next day, which is faster than Plan X even with all roads open. The survey teams are still needed on the ground to reach people and check the places the images show as flooded.
s: (a) Names disaster management
(b) Bhuvan and Cartosat; two of terrain, soil, land use, vegetation
(c) Finds 16 a day, 2.5 so 3 days, and explains the cut roads
(d) Chooses Plan Y first, with the teams for ground work

questions.q: A letter in a Thiruvananthapuram newspaper argues that India should stop launching satellites because of the space debris problem. A reader wants to reply. (a) How does space debris form? (b) Give two dangers of space debris. (c) Name one ISRO mission that studies objects in space and one ISRO satellite series whose images help people on the ground. (d) What are countries now doing about the debris problem? (e) Should launches stop, as the letter says? Give your judgement and justify it using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) After their useful life, many satellites and their rocket parts are left in space as space junk or debris. (b) It crowds space and could collide with working satellites; larger pieces can crash on the ground instead of burning up in the atmosphere. (c) Space: AstroSat, Aditya L1, Chandrayaan or Mangalyaan; ground: Cartosat. (d) They are working together to remove this dangerous debris. (e) Launches should not simply stop: satellites do jobs we depend on, such as communication, weather monitoring and disaster management; the better answer is to keep working together to remove the debris, as countries now do.
s: (a) Explains debris as old satellites and rocket parts left in space
(b) Gives collision risk and crash risk
(c) Names one space-study mission and Cartosat
(d) Countries working together to remove debris
(e) Gives a judgement that weighs the satellites' uses against the debris, with removal as the remedy
